desc:
You are given a long string s and a list of words, written as one string words in which the words are separated by commas, for example "ace,aec,bb".

Return how many words of the list are a subsequence of s. A word that appears several times in the list is counted once per appearance.

For example, for s = "abcde" and words = "a,bb,acd,ace,ace" the answer is 4: a, acd and both copies of ace fit, bb does not.
constraints: The list has 1 to 1,500 words; each word has 1 to 20 lowercase letters
s consists of lowercase letters; words contains lowercase letters and commas only, with no empty word
hints: Testing each word separately with two pointers is correct. Think about what it costs when there are many words and s is long.
Scan s only once. For every word, remember which letter it is waiting for next, and group the words by that letter.
When you read a letter c from s, take the whole group waiting for c, advance each word by one letter and put it into the group of its new waiting letter. Words that run out of letters are matches.
editorial: The direct approach checks every word against s with two pointers, which costs O(|s|) per word in the worst case, so O(|s| · W) overall. That is fine for small inputs but wasteful when s is long.

Instead, process s a single time and keep 26 buckets. Bucket c holds the words (with a progress index) whose next unmatched letter is c. For each letter c of s we empty bucket c; each word in it advances one letter, and is either counted as matched (no letters left) or moved to the bucket of its new next letter. Every letter of every word is moved at most once, so the total work is O(|s| + total length of the words).
